summary: The forecast's validation machinery is serious by the standard of published election models. Every layer is graded leave-one-cycle-out on eight Knesset elections at up to four horizons, with proper scores (the interval score and the Brier score), multiple seeds, a fixed list mask, adversarial leak audits and written disclosures. The literature supports the core design. The harness's interval score is exactly the Gneiting-Raftery proper score for central intervals, the Brier score is the standard binary score, blocking folds by election follows Roberts et al. and the leave-one-group-out logic of Vehtari, Gelman and Gabry, the site's 'calibrated first, then sharp' framing is Gneiting-Balabdaoui-Raftery's, and NUTS with divergence monitoring is standard practice. The literature challenges current practice in five places. (1) Calibration. At the published horizon the intervals are not 'conservative' but too wide: the 90% bands cover 98-99% of list results at eve, D-7 and D-21 on the s.46 yardstick. On that yardstick every leave-one-cycle-out fold picks a residual width of 0.6-0.7, and 0.6 beats the shipped 0.9 on MAE, threshold Brier and interval score. The shipping gate 'must not lose coverage' blocks the move toward 90% because it scores any drop from 98% as a loss. Some of the excess is an artefact of integer seat counts (Czado-Gneiting-Held) and should be measured with a discrete PIT. (2) Selection. There are 32 arms in the eve harness, 54 proposals and 14 candidates in round five, an Arab arm chosen among nine, three baseline restatements in three days, and a two-route shipping rule whose fold route counts |d| < 0.1 as a tie, so a layer that fires in two cycles passes with 2 wins and 6 ties. Varma and Simon, Gelman and Loken, the Bayesian Workflow and Diebold all say that grading choices on the record that selected them overstates performance. The remedies are one pre-declared primary proper score, a paired fold test with a seed-noise floor, nested leave-one-cycle-out for any arm picked from variants, and a frozen, pre-registered 2026 forecast scored after 27 October. (3) Time direction. Leave-one-cycle-out lets 2019-2022 set the parameters used to grade 2009-2015 (Burkner, Gabry and Vehtari). A leave-future-out grade should sit beside it, and the site sentence 'using only the polls published before each date' should say that the layer parameters come from the other seven elections. (4) What is scored. The graded point estimate (per-list median seats) is not the one published (the median share vector, allocated), which is 0.05-0.07 seats per list worse, and 'median beats mean' is guaranteed by absolute-error scoring (Gneiting 2011). All scores are per-list marginals, so the dependence layers that drive P(NB>=61) are graded only through a bloc Brier on eight outcomes. WIS over eleven levels and energy or variogram scores would use the record better. Gelman, Hullman, Wlezien and Morris show why eight elections cannot certify a 14% probability. (5) Computation and communication. The production gates (r-hat <= 1.02, bulk ESS >= 300, one reseed) are looser than Vehtari et al.'s standard (r-hat < 1.01, bulk and tail ESS > 400). The 14 October fit had ESS 261, and sigma_g does not mix at harness draw counts. The fake-data recovery is a single August replicate on an older model, and the PSIS-LOO ladder carried undisclosed Pareto-k warnings. Headline probabilities move by up to 1.3 points across projection seeds, so a decimal place overstates precision. Win probabilities read as more certain than vote shares (Westwood, Messing and Lelkes), and quantile dotplots improve decisions (Fernandes et al.). Nine challenges below turn these into harness or evidence-class tests.

findings.claim: A scoring rule is strictly proper when issuing one's true predictive distribution uniquely maximises the expected score, so proper scores reward careful, honest forecasts. For a central (1 - alpha) prediction interval [l, u] the proper score is the interval score S = (u - l) + (2/alpha)(l - x)1{x < l} + (2/alpha)(x - u)1{x > u}: a narrow interval is rewarded and every unit by which the outcome misses is charged 2/alpha. In the paper's case study three 95% interval forecasts all had close to nominal coverage, the sharpest was not the best, and the interval score (not coverage) ranked them.
findings.quant: Eq. (43), Section 6.2, p. 370; case study Section 6.3 and Table 2, p. 371 (100,000 one-step forecasts of a bilinear process). Model: validate_bayes.py and validate_horizon.py compute exactly this score at alpha = 0.10, i.e. (hi - lo) + 20 x miss in seats. Restated baseline (CLR latent, ballot-fidelity windows, 3 seeds, dossier s.46): eve 9.280, D-7 9.430, D-21 9.622 seats per list.

findings.claim: Brier proposed scoring probability forecasts of a binary event by the mean squared difference between the stated probability and the 0/1 outcome (0 is perfect, lower is better). It is the standard verification score for yes/no events and is what the model uses for threshold passage and for the bloc-majority probability. Because it is an average over events, pooling many near-certain events (lists sure to pass) shrinks it without saying anything about the hard cases, so it needs a stratified or skill-score companion.
findings.quant: Monthly Weather Review 78(1):1-3. Model: pooled threshold Brier .0474 at eve on the s.46 yardstick averages 9-13 lists per cycle, most with p ~ 1 and outcome 1. On straddlers alone the same machinery scored 0.226 (D-56) and 0.234 (D-21) after the new-straddler layer (s.36), about five times the pooled figure. Bloc P(NB>=61) Brier over 8 outcomes, from model_validation_bayes.csv and model_validation_horizon.csv (13 Oct runs): eve 0.030 (se 0.010), D-7 0.037 (se 0.016), D-21 0.058 (se 0.029), D-56 0.158 (se 0.062). A constant base-rate forecast (3 of 8) scores 0.234.

findings.claim: Probabilistic forecasts should maximise sharpness subject to calibration. Calibration (statistical consistency between forecasts and outcomes) comes first, and among calibrated forecasts the sharper one is better. A hump-shaped PIT or rank histogram signals overdispersed forecasts whose prediction intervals are too wide on average, and sharpness is read from the average width of the central 50% and 90% intervals. Over-coverage is therefore a calibration failure, not a safety margin.
findings.quant: Summary p. 243; PIT shapes p. 253; Section 3.3 (sharpness via 50% and 90% interval widths) p. 255. Model: 90% coverage .981 (eve), .990 (D-7) and .990 (D-21) on the s.46 yardstick. In the 13 Oct horizon file 7 of 8 cycles cover 100% at both D-7 and D-21, with 1-2 misses in about 91 list-cycles where 9 are expected (binomial P(<=1 miss | 10%) = 0.0008, ignoring within-cycle dependence). s.46 width grid: every leave-one-cycle-out fold picks a residual width of 0.6 or 0.7. At 0.6 the scores are MAE 1.609, Brier .043, interval score 8.773 and coverage .960, all better than the shipped 0.9 (1.626 / .047 / 9.302 / .981).

findings.claim: When forecasts are issued as central intervals, the weighted interval score (WIS) combines the absolute error of the median with interval scores at K levels, using weights w0 = 1/2 and wk = alpha_k/2. It is proper for any non-negative weights, approximates the CRPS as K grows, generalises absolute error, and decomposes into a dispersion term plus over- and under-prediction penalties. The COVID-19 Forecast Hub scores the median plus K = 11 intervals (nominal 98%, 95%, 90%, ..., 10%). Inverse-U PIT histograms mark overdispersed forecasts.
findings.quant: Eqs. (1)-(3) and the Forecast Hub specification (arXiv 2005.12881, p. 4); PIT discussion p. 9. Model: the harness scores one level only (90%, alpha = 0.10). The 50% and 80% ranges, where most list outcomes are decided, are never graded.

findings.claim: For count (ordered discrete) outcomes the ordinary probability integral transform is not uniform even when the model is correct, so calibration checks designed for continuous variables mislead. The authors give a nonrandomised PIT histogram, marginal calibration diagrams and proper scores (such as the predictive deviance) for counts, usable with any Bayesian or classical model.
findings.quant: Biometrics 65(4):1254-1261. Model: seats are integers, and harness coverage counts a hit when the actual count is >= the 5th and <= the 95th percentile of integer seat draws. A calibrated discrete forecast therefore covers at least 90%, usually more, and a list whose range starts at 0 is covered whenever it fails. Part of the 98-99% coverage is this artefact. The rest is real overdispersion, which the s.46 interval-score gains from narrower widths show.

findings.claim: Point forecasts are meaningful only when the scoring function is fixed in advance, or the forecaster is told which functional (mean, median, quantile) to report, and the scoring function must be consistent for that functional. Mismatches can produce grossly misguided comparisons. Quantiles, including the median, are elicited by generalised piecewise-linear scores such as absolute error; means are elicited by Bregman scores such as squared error.
findings.quant: JASA 106(494):746-762 (abstract). Model: s.28 reports the median beating the mean by ~0.09 seats per list 'in every configuration'. Under absolute-error scoring that is the expected result, not independent evidence. The published central count is a third object (the median share vector, renormalised and D'Hondt-allocated). MAE per list in the 13 Oct horizon harness, published central vs per-list seat median: D-7 1.696 vs 1.628, D-21 1.887 vs 1.831, D-56 2.558 vs 2.511. The shipping rule grades the per-list median, not what the site prints.

findings.claim: Few proper scores exist for multivariate forecasts. The energy score is the usual choice for sample (ensemble) forecasts but has limited power to detect a wrongly specified correlation between components. Variogram-based scores, built from pairwise differences between components, were distinctly more sensitive to errors in the correlation structure in simulations and in a five-site wind case study. They are proper but not strictly proper, so the authors use them alongside other scores.
findings.quant: Monthly Weather Review 143(4):1321-1334 (abstract). Model: every harness score is per list (marginal), except the bloc Brier on 8 binary outcomes. The dependence features (the t(5) bloc swing, gevalt coupling, the satellite-sourced trailing-Likud beat and the Arab family term) move P(NB>=61) by several points (s.41: 20.9 -> 13.5 from the satellite sourcing alone), yet they are graded only through marginals.

findings.claim: Election forecasts are hard to evaluate for calibration. 95% intervals cannot be checked even on 10 back-tested elections, and sub-unit results are correlated, so pooling them adds less than it seems. Implausible conditional predictions are a practical check. They can come from adding independent long-tailed errors on top of a correlated model, which lowers the effective correlation, and the authors found bugs in their own model by inspecting such predictions. Because calibration is so hard to verify, forecasters face incentives toward underconfidence, which hedges against the reputational cost of a miss. FiveThirtyEight's political 20% events happened 14% of the time and its 80% events 88%.
findings.quant: Judgment and Decision Making 15(5):863-880. Section 2.1 (difficulty of calibration) p. 866; implausible predictions and correlation p. 868; incentives and the 538 calibration figures p. 873. Model: 8 graded elections, with the bloc P(NB>=61) graded on 8 outcomes. If the 2026 headline (~13-14%) were exactly calibrated, eight such forecasts would see no NB majority 30% of the time (0.86^8), so the record cannot tell 14% from 5% or 25%. The independent per-list residual shock (x1.35 for first-cycle lists) sits on top of a t(5) bloc swing, which is the structure the paper flags.

findings.site_use: Eight elections cannot certify a 14% probability. The record checks the machinery list by list, and the bloc number should be read with that limit in mind (Gelman, Hullman, Wlezien & Morris 2020).

findings.claim: Calibration means that events given X% happen about X% of the time across many forecasts; FiveThirtyEight checks it over thousands of its own forecasts since 2008. Calibration alone is not skill: giving every NCAA team a 1-in-68 chance is calibrated and useless, so FiveThirtyEight also reports Brier skill scores. Its election forecasts have historically leaned underconfident.
findings.quant: FiveThirtyEight, 4 Apr 2019: of 5,589 events forecast near 70%, 71% happened; of 55,853 events near 5%, 4% happened; in elections, candidates given ~75% won ~83%. Model: the only near-adequate samples for a calibration check are list-level threshold passage (~90 list-cycles) and the formation outcomes (8).

findings.site_use: A good probabilistic forecast is first calibrated (things it calls 70% likely happen about 70% of the time) and then sharp. This is the standard FiveThirtyEight applies to its own record (Silver 2019).

findings.claim: In survey experiments, people shown a win probability were more confident about who was ahead and who would win than people shown a vote-share projection with a margin of error, and participants in every format misjudged the chance of winning. In an incentivised voting game, higher win probabilities (but not larger vote-share leads) reduced paying to vote. Small vote-share leads map to large win probabilities, which readers misread.
findings.quant: Journal of Politics 82(4):1530-1544 (Oct 2020). Study 1 n = 4,151 (hypothetical Senate race, three formats); study 2 n = 1,171 (economic game). Design and n from the Pew Research summary of 6 Feb 2018; citation from Crossref.

findings.claim: In a repeated decision experiment on transit predictions, quantile dotplots (50 discrete outcomes) and CDF plots led to better and more consistent decisions than textual interval displays. Dotplots reached about 97% of the optimal expected payoff, 5 points above the no-uncertainty control. Text displays were sensitive to which interval level was communicated.
findings.quant: Proc. ACM CHI 2018; dotplot gain over control +5 percentage points of optimal payoff (95% CI 2 to 8); within-subject SD 4 points lower than control.

findings.claim: When data have temporal, spatial or hierarchical structure, random cross-validation seriously underestimates predictive error. Folds should be blocked on the dependence structure, even when fitted residuals look uncorrelated, though blocking can force extrapolation and so overstate error.
findings.quant: Ecography 40(8):913-929, abstract p. 913. Model: whole cycles are the right block. But 2019a, 2019s, 2020 and 2021 fell within 23 months with largely the same lists, so those four folds are not independent of each other; s.43 notes that the Arab slope k 'rests on 2019a'.

findings.claim: For time series, leave-one-out cross-validation lets future observations inform predictions of the past, so it is over-optimistic as a measure of forecasting skill. Leave-future-out cross-validation respects time order, and Pareto-smoothed importance sampling can approximate it without one refit per step.
findings.quant: Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation 90(14):2499-2523 (2020), abstract. Model: when 2015 is graded, the trailing-Likud mean comes from 2019a and 2019s (only 3 trailing years exist; s.36). The Arab a and k, the new-straddler drift and the industry shocks also borrow later elections. The site says each election 'was forecast again ... using only the polls published before each date', which is true of the polls but not of these parameters.

findings.claim: When cross-validation is used both to tune a model and to report its error, the reported error is substantially optimistic. On null datasets with no real signal, tuned classifiers showed low CV error while their independent-test performance was at chance. Nested CV (tuning inside an inner loop, error estimated in an outer loop) was nearly unbiased, so every selection step must be repeated inside each fold.
findings.quant: BMC Bioinformatics 7:91 (2006), abstract: the tuned shrunken-centroid classifier's CV error was below 30% on 18.5% of null training sets. Model: arab_regB was chosen among nine graded arms (s.43c), trail_sat among five variants (s.41) and the residual width from a 6-point grid, each graded on the folds that chose it. The exception is the width grid's printed 'LOO width choices', which is already a nested selection.

findings.claim: Even without deliberate fishing, analysis choices that would have gone differently had the data come out differently create a 'garden of forking paths': many implicit comparisons, whose winner looks better than it is.
findings.quant: American Scientist 102(6):460 (2014). Model: 32 named arms sit in validate_bayes.ABLATIONS today, and round five merged 54 proposals into 14 candidates (s.41). The baseline was restated three times between 13 and 15 Oct (s.41, s.43, s.46), and each new candidate is graded against the latest one. The trailing-Likud ramp passed the fold route on one harness (2 wins, 6 ties) and failed the Brier gate on the other (s.46).

findings.claim: Pre-registration, which fixes the questions and the analysis plan before the outcomes are seen, separates testing predictions from generating postdictions, a line that hindsight bias otherwise blurs. Partial strategies keep it usable when the data already exist.

The combine plan's G1/G2 gates were applied as written and dropped the ramp (s.46). The undecided half-weight was fixed in advance (s.11). The 2026 election is the one truly unseen outcome.

findings.claim: The Diebold-Mariano test was meant for comparing forecasts, not models. The belief that pseudo-out-of-sample analysis is the best insurance against in-sample overfitting in model comparison is largely false, and in finite samples it widens the scope for data mining (for example over the choice of sample split). Its legitimate use is learning about comparative historical predictive performance.
findings.quant: JBES 33(1):1-9 (2015); NBER WP 18391 (2012), abstract and the discussion of split-point mining (WP PDF p. 13). Model: the eight-cycle harness is a pseudo-out-of-sample exercise used as the model-selection device, so its numbers for the shipped configuration are selection-affected.

findings.claim: Election forecasts built on a few historical elections usually overstate their certainty, because they ignore uncertainty in coefficient estimates and in specification choices; with limited data, many models are empirically justifiable. Once those sources were accounted for, 95% intervals widened to about +/-10 points of vote share at the state level and +/-7 nationally.
findings.quant: International Journal of Forecasting 31(3):965-979, abstract p. 965 and p. 966. Model: the Arab term uses full-sample point values a = -0.634 (se 0.41) and k = 0.247 (se 0.21), n = 8 (s.43 b, d). The trailing-Likud beat is drawn as Normal(LOO mean, sd) from n = 3 (mean +5.0, sd 4.9; s.36) without the mean's own standard error (~2.8). The new-straddler drift of -1.6 pp comes from 11 lists and re-measured at -0.33 pp on vote shares (s.41).

findings.claim: Rank-normalised split-R-hat should be below 1.01 (the old 1.1 rule passes chains that have not converged), with at least four chains. Rank-normalised bulk ESS should exceed 400 for stable Monte Carlo standard errors. When intervals or quantiles are reported, the tail-ESS (at the 5% and 95% quantiles) must also be adequate, and the MCSE should be checked for every quantity of interest.
findings.quant: Bayesian Analysis 16(2):667-718; arXiv version Section 2 (recommendations), pp. 4-5. Model: REFIT_GATES are r-hat <= 1.02 and bulk ESS >= 300, bulk only (bayes_model.py). findings.claim: Divergent transitions flag regions of high curvature that the numerical integrator cannot resolve. Any divergence should prompt suspicion of the estimates, and divergences that persist as the step size shrinks indicate bias that calls for reparameterisation (for example non-centred forms) or stronger priors. These diagnostics are necessary but not sufficient for valid inference.

findings.claim: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling stabilises importance weights, and its fitted Pareto shape k-hat is a reliability diagnostic. Estimates are trustworthy when k-hat < min(1 - 1/log10(S), 0.7). Above 0.7 they should not be trusted, and the affected leave-one-out folds should be refit exactly (PSIS-LOO+) or replaced by K-fold CV.

challenges.title: The intervals are miscalibrated, not 'conservative': retune the width and change the coverage gate
challenges.what_literature_says: Sharpness should be maximised subject to calibration, and over-coverage (a hump-shaped PIT) means the intervals are too wide (F03). Coverage is not a proper score; the interval score ranks intervals that have equal coverage (F01). Integer outcomes inflate coverage counted with inclusive percentiles (F05). Underconfidence is the documented bias created by forecasters' incentives, and it is visible in FiveThirtyEight's political record (F08, F09).
challenges.current_model: On the s.46 yardstick the 90% intervals cover .981 / .990 / .990 at eve / D-7 / D-21. In the s.46 width grid every leave-one-cycle-out fold picks residual width 0.6-0.7, and 0.6 beats the shipped 0.9 on MAE, threshold Brier and interval score while still covering .960. RESID_SCALE stays at 0.9. The s.46 gate ('must not lose coverage') and harness_compare.py ('without losing coverage') count any drop from 98% as a loss, even a move toward the 90% target. The site calls over-coverage 'conservative' and still says 0.9 'wins every leave-one-cycle-out fold', which was true on the older harness but is not on the s.46 yardstick.
challenges.proposed_change: (1) Replace 'must not lose coverage' with 'must not move coverage further from 0.90', with a tolerance band (for about 91 list-cycles the binomial 95% band is 0.84-0.96; widen it for within-cycle dependence with a cycle bootstrap). (2) Make the weighted interval score the interval criterion. (3) Run the RESID_SCALE recalibration candidate (0.6 / 0.7) with a nested leave-one-cycle-out choice at eve, D-7, D-21 and, once the CLR caches exist, D-56. (4) Rewrite the site caption and the '0.9 wins every fold' sentence.
challenges.how_to_test: Harness: width grid on harness_cache_clr_fidelity scored by WIS, nonrandomised PIT and straddler Brier, with the width chosen on 7 folds and graded on the 8th. Ship if pooled WIS and threshold Brier improve and median MAE does not worsen beyond seed noise (5 seeds).

challenges.title: Shipping rule: one pre-declared proper score, a paired fold test, nested selection, no OR clause
challenges.what_literature_says: Selecting among variants on the same folds that grade them biases the reported error (F15, F24). Forking paths make the winner of many implicit comparisons look better than it is (F16). Pseudo-out-of-sample comparison does not by itself insure against overfitting (F18). Comparisons should carry the standard error of the paired difference (F12). Pre-registration separates prediction from postdiction (F17).
challenges.current_model: harness_compare.py: a layer ships when it wins or ties median-seat MAE in every fold, OR wins the pooled score on every metric without losing coverage. Ties are |d| < 0.1 seat (s.46), so a layer that fires in two cycles passes the fold route with 2 wins and 6 ties (one-sided sign test on the non-tied folds, p = 0.25). arab_regB shipped on the pooled route with folds 4 / 2 / 2 (sign test on the six non-tied folds, p = 0.34) after nine arms were graded. The fold criterion is a point score (median MAE), and the pooled route's coverage clause rewards over-coverage. 32 arms are in ABLATIONS, and the baseline was restated three times in three days.
challenges.proposed_change: (1) Declare one primary score before grading: pooled WIS per list, plus log score on threshold passage for lists with 0.02 < p < 0.98, plus the bloc log score at fixed weights; the other metrics stay descriptive. (2) Use a single route: a sign-flip permutation test across the 8 folds on the primary score (minimum attainable one-sided p is 1/256), at least 5 projection seeds, and a pooled gain larger than twice the seed-to-seed SD. (3) Grade any arm chosen among variants by nested leave-one-cycle-out. (4) Record the number of arms tried beside every shipped change. (5) Before 27 Oct, freeze the final configuration and the 2026 scoring plan with a timestamped hash.
challenges.how_to_test: Re-grade this round's shipped changes (trail_sat, gone14_zero, pair_fix, arab_regB, clr_latent) under the proposed rule on the cached posteriors (no refits) and report which would have shipped. Evidence class: harness.

challenges.title: Publish a leave-future-out grade beside leave-one-cycle-out
challenges.what_literature_says: For time-ordered data, leave-one-out lets the future inform the past and is optimistic for forecasting skill; leave-future-out is the time-respecting check (F14). Blocks should follow the dependence structure (F13), and LOO comparisons should carry standard errors (F12).
challenges.current_model: Industry shocks, the trailing-Likud mean, the new-straddler drift, the Arab a and k, and the firm scorecards are all estimated from the seven other cycles, including later ones. The site says each election was forecast 'using only the polls published before each date'.
challenges.proposed_change: Add a past_only flag to decompose(), trailing_likud_params, new_straddler_params, arab_turnout_params and the firm lambda scorecards. Grade 2013-2022 with parameters from earlier cycles only, switching off layers that have no prior data, and publish both grades. Amend the site sentence.
challenges.how_to_test: Harness on the cached eve / D-7 / D-21 posteriors (projection only, no refits); compare pooled metrics on the 7 common folds and report the LFO minus LOCO gap.

challenges.title: Grade the point estimate the site publishes, and state the loss
challenges.what_literature_says: A point forecast must be scored with a function consistent for the functional it reports. Under absolute error the median wins by construction (F06).
challenges.current_model: The shipping rule grades per-list seat medians (seat_mae_median). The site prints the central allocation from the median share vector, renormalised and D'Hondt-allocated, which is 0.05-0.07 seats per list worse at D-7, D-21 and D-56 in the 13 Oct horizon harness. s.28 presents 'median beats mean' as evidence.
challenges.proposed_change: Either make seat_mae_central the graded point metric (add it to the eve ablation CSV and to harness_compare), or publish per-list medians with a note that they need not sum to 120. State on the site that the central count targets absolute seat error.
challenges.how_to_test: Add seat_mae_central to validate_bayes.py ablation rows; re-grade the s.41-s.46 ship decisions on it and report any that flip.

challenges.title: Score whole distributions and the joint outcome, not one interval per list
challenges.what_literature_says: WIS over K = 11 levels approximates the CRPS and uses the whole distribution (F04). Marginal scores cannot see wrong correlations; variogram and energy scores can (F07). A pooled Brier is dominated by easy events (F02). Calibration of a bloc probability cannot be established from 8 elections (F08).
challenges.current_model: The harness scores a single 90% interval, a threshold Brier pooled over every list, and a bloc Brier over 8 outcomes. No score targets the joint seat vector, even though the bloc swing, gevalt coupling and trailing-Likud sourcing are dependence layers that move P(NB>=61) by several points.
challenges.proposed_change: Save per-cycle seat draws (or 23 quantiles) from the harness. From them compute WIS(K = 11), the ranked probability score for integer seats, pooled nonrandomised PIT histograms, a straddler-only Brier with a skill score against a poll-average reference, and energy and variogram scores on the seat vector and on the three bloc totals. On the site, show reliability bins with their counts.
challenges.how_to_test: One harness pass on the cached posteriors that writes draws; compare shipped, latent_only and no_swing on the variogram score to check whether the bloc swing earns its place on a joint score. Evidence class: harness.

challenges.title: Convergence gates and Monte Carlo error at the published standard
challenges.what_literature_says: R-hat < 1.01; bulk and tail ESS > 400; MCSE for every reported quantity (F20). Divergences are necessary but not sufficient diagnostics (F22). NUTS is the standard sampler (F21).
challenges.current_model: REFIT_GATES are r-hat <= 1.02 and bulk ESS >= 300 (no tail-ESS), with one reseed allowed. The 14 Oct fit had ESS 261 and r-hat 1.02. Harness sigma_g r-hat is 1.07-1.79 at 400-600 draws. The site prints 'r-hat <= 1.02'. P(NB>=61) is published to a decimal, while projection seeds move it by up to 1.3 points (SD 0.67 pp on the ALR posterior).
challenges.proposed_change: Set the gates to r-hat < 1.01 and bulk and tail ESS >= 400 on the endpoint shares, tau, final-week house effects and the derived P(NB>=61). Run longer chains (for example 4 x 2000) instead of reseeding. If sigma_g still mixes poorly, non-centre the group-level house effects or raise the harness draws, and report fold-level r-hat. Report the MCSE of headline probabilities from at least 5 projection seeds and round them to whole percent.
challenges.how_to_test: Refit 2026 at 4 x 2000 and compute tail-ESS; run 10 projection seeds for the P(NB>=61) MCSE. Refit the harness folds where sigma_g r-hat > 1.01 with more draws and check whether the graded metrics move. Evidence class: computation diagnostics.

challenges.title: Propagate the estimation uncertainty of layers fitted on a handful of elections
challenges.what_literature_says: Forecasts built on few elections overstate certainty when they ignore coefficient and specification uncertainty (F19).
challenges.current_model: Arab term: full-sample point values a = -0.634 (se 0.41) and k = 0.247 (se 0.21), n = 8. Trailing-Likud: Normal(mean +5.0, sd 4.9) from n = 3, with no uncertainty in the mean. New straddler: -1.6 pp from 11 lists, re-measured at -0.33 pp on vote shares.
challenges.proposed_change: In each simulation draw (a, k) from their joint sampling distribution (or from the 8 strict-LOO fits); draw the trailing-Likud shift from a predictive t with 2 df and scale sd x sqrt(1 + 1/n); do the same for the new-straddler drift.
challenges.how_to_test: Horizon harness at D-7 / D-21 on WIS, coverage and threshold Brier. Expect wider intervals for the affected lists, which interacts with challenge 1, so grade the two jointly. Evidence class: harness.

challenges.title: Model checking: targeted predictive checks, a refreshed fake-data/SBC run, and Pareto-k disclosure
challenges.what_literature_says: Posterior predictive checks should use discrepancies that target what the model is used for (F23). Fake-data simulation and simulation-based calibration validate the computation (F24). PSIS-LOO estimates with k-hat > 0.7 are unreliable and need exact refits (F25).
challenges.current_model: The PPC is a single in-sample coverage number (~98% inside a 95% envelope band). Fake-data recovery was run once, on 29 Aug, on the ALR model with 6 lists x 20 weeks. The PSIS-LOO ladder carried warning = True for three of four models, and the workflow doc does not disclose it.
challenges.proposed_change: (1) Add PPC discrepancies: the per-firm mean residual in the final 14 days, lag-1 autocorrelation of within-firm residuals, and the dispersion of final-week polls around the latent, each with a posterior predictive p-value. (2) Compute LOO-PIT for poll observations via PSIS and report k-hat. (3) Re-run workflow_bayes recovery on the CLR production model at 21 lists x 45 weeks with at least 50 replicates (an SBC-style rank check on tau, endpoint shares and house effects). (4) Disclose the PSIS warnings and use K-fold CV by week block where k-hat > 0.7.
challenges.how_to_test: Evidence class: model checking, outside the harness. Pass if the SBC rank histograms are uniform (chi-square) and no PPC p-value falls below 0.01 or above 0.99.

challenges.title: Communicate probabilities with their precision and their seat basis
challenges.what_literature_says: Win probabilities read as more certain than vote shares and can demobilise readers (F10). Quantile dotplots and CDFs beat text intervals for decisions (F11). Eight elections cannot certify a bloc probability (F08). Monte Carlo error should be reported (F20).
challenges.current_model: The headline P(NB>=61) is given to a decimal (e.g. 14.5), with PM probabilities alongside and 90% ranges as bars and text.
challenges.proposed_change: Round headline probabilities to whole percent and note the Monte Carlo error. Show the bloc total as a 50-dot quantile dotplot. Put the seat range next to every probability. Add one sentence on what eight elections can and cannot certify.
challenges.how_to_test: Evidence class: communication research; no harness test. Optional: a small reader test of probability vs dotplot comprehension.

open_questions: No peer-reviewed evaluation of Israeli seat forecasts was located. The only peer-reviewed review covering Israeli poll performance found (Kenett, Pfeffermann & Steinberg 2018, Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application 5:1-24) was verified at abstract level only and is not used as a finding.
How much of the 98-99% coverage is discreteness (integer seats, lists at zero) and how much is genuine overdispersion? Answering this needs saved harness draws and a nonrandomised PIT.

Should the residual width be tuned for seat MAE (the owner's stated objective) or for interval calibration? The two can diverge through the threshold nonlinearity, and the loss should be declared before grading (Gneiting 2011). On the s.46 yardstick they agree on 0.6-0.7.
Within-cycle dependence makes binomial coverage bands too narrow. Should the coverage tolerance come from a cycle-level bootstrap?
D-56 CLR-fidelity caches do not exist yet (s.46), so the eight-weeks-out accuracy figures on the site are still on the older ALR yardstick.
Should the frozen pre-election configuration be published (for example a hashed file on the site) or kept in the repository only? This is an owner decision.
